title: Alert Bay residents question police actions
article: After a domestic dispute ended with their neighbour Lorraine Jacobson being shot dead by police Const. Russ Chanin, grieving and fearful residents will ask some tough questions of RCMP at a community meeting tonight.

"I called 911 and they were supposed to protect her ... instead they killed her ... it makes me feel I killed my friend," said Melinda McKay, who called police Friday when Jacobson and Ernie Joseph were arguing and throwing pebbles at each other in the Whe la la U subdivision. "You wouldn't think this would happen in a nice village ... it makes me afraid to call 911."
The first police officer on the scene that night was Chanin, and police say he was confronted by 40-year-old Jacobson, who "was brandishing a large butcher knife."
She ignored an order to put the knife down, efforts to disarm her failed, and Chanin fired a single shot into her chest, says a police press release.
McKay insists the knife was more like a paring knife, and she and other community members wonder why no warning shots were fired.

"I only heard one shot ... why no warning?" asked McKay. Jacobson, a single mother, leaves behind three children, an adult son Jody, 11-year-old Lance and nine-year-old Summer, a girl who was in the house when her mother was shot.
The community is holding a memorial service each night until Jacobson's funeral Saturday in Vancouver.

Kelly Scheck, another Whe la la U resident, was "devastated" by the incident, but added that the community is "hurt and angry" at the same time. "She was a new community member but she was such a nice person who would never hurt anyone."
Many other residents of the neighbourhood are concerned by the incident, including Shirley Robinson, who lives in the other half of the duplex where the shooting took place.
"I have an eight-month-old daughter here and there were bullets flying. I think the police over-reacted, big time."
Robinson's mother, Darlene Coon, who is staying with her until the fear dies down, says First Nations people should be involved in policing their own neighbourhoods.
"We used to have our own patrols, but the funding was cut," she said. "This is really scary, I mean it ... who do we turn to in cases like these?"
Speaking for the RCMP, Sgt. Lee Omilusik said police are just as distressed as citizens, and will attend the meeting to answer as many questions as possible.
